statement.p: Convert the integral \int_0^{\sqrt{10}}\int_{-x}^x\,dy\,dx to polar coordinates and evaluate it (use t for \theta):
With a = , b = , c = and d = ,

static.solution: -\pi/4\le\theta\le\pi/4. Also, the outer (right) boundary of the region is \sqrt{10} = x = r\cos\theta. Hence, 0\le r\le \sqrt{10}/\cos\theta. The integral becomes \int_0^{\sqrt{10}}\int_{-x}^x\,dy\,dx =\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\int_0^{\sqrt{10}/\!\cos\theta}\,r\,dr\,d\theta. Then \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\int_0^{\sqrt{10}/\!\cos\theta}\,r\,dr\,d\theta = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(\frac{r^2}{2}\bigg|_0^{\sqrt{10}/\!\cos\theta}\right)\,d\theta = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{5}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta. And \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{5}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta =5 \tan\theta\bigg|_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = 5\cdot(1 - (-1)) = 10. Notice that we can check this answer because the integral gives the area of the shaded triangular region which is \frac{1}{2} \cdot \sqrt{10} \cdot (2\sqrt{10}) = 10.
